note: These are v0 evals. They exist to make the skill testable and to invite community contributions. Each case describes a realistic scenario and the shape of output that a good application of the skill should produce. PRs adding cases, sharpening assertions, or reporting cases where the skill fails are welcome. Run with skill-creator's harness or by hand — an assertion that fails is data, not a defect in the eval.

evals.name: post-mortem-collapsed-DQ-and-OQ
evals.prompt: We launched a new pricing tier six months ago. Revenue is up 40%. Everyone's celebrating and the CEO wants me to write a retro on 'what we did right.' I have a nagging feeling we got lucky — a big competitor raised prices two weeks after our launch and we absorbed a lot of their spillover. How should I write this retro?
evals.expected_output: Output should (a) explicitly separate decision quality from outcome quality — praise the outcome without collapsing it into process validation; (b) name resulting as the trap the current 'what we did right' framing risks falling into; (c) reference Pete Carroll or a similar canonical resulting case; (d) suggest un-collapsing the two by asking what would have happened if the competitor hadn't raised prices; (e) recommend a decision-journal practice for future decisions so this reconstruction problem is smaller next time; (f) end with a concrete testable action (e.g., a specific reframing of the retro's opening question); (g) cite Duke / Thinking in Bets or How to Decide.
assertions: Output explicitly names the distinction between decision quality (DQ) and outcome quality (OQ), or 'resulting' as a term
Output takes seriously the user's nagging feeling — treats it as signal, not doubt to be reassured away
Output references at least one Duke case (Pete Carroll canonical) OR names the general resulting pattern
Output challenges the CEO's 'what we did right' framing rather than accepting it uncritically
Output recommends a decision-journal or written-record practice
Output cites Annie Duke, Thinking in Bets, or How to Decide by name at least once
Output ends with a specific testable action, not a general homily
Output does NOT collapse into 'trust your gut' or generic post-mortem advice

evals.name: kill-criteria-for-a-current-project
evals.prompt: I've been running a side product for 14 months. It has 200 paying users, $6k MRR, 20% MoM growth for the last three months. I keep telling myself 'if it's not clearly working by summer, I'll wind it down' but I know that's not real — summer will come and I'll rationalize whatever the numbers say. How do I set an actual kill criterion?
evals.expected_output: Output should (a) diagnose the 'clearly working' phrasing as unobservable and therefore not a real kill criterion; (b) walk through Duke's state + date format explicitly; (c) push for observable state (a specific metric with a specific threshold) and a binding date (specific calendar day); (d) name the precommitment gap — that setting the criterion isn't enough, needs a quitting coach and a written commitment; (e) reference Everest 1996 or a similar case where kill criteria failed under emotional load; (f) end with the user actually writing the criterion right now — not deferring; (g) cite Duke / Quit.
assertions: Output names Duke's exact format for a kill criterion: state + date
Output diagnoses the user's current phrasing ('clearly working') as unobservable and therefore not a real kill criterion
Output pushes for a specific observable metric with a specific threshold
Output pushes for a binding calendar date, not a season or quarter
Output addresses the precommitment problem — that writing the criterion is not enough; needs a quitting coach or external accountability
Output references Everest 1996 OR another case where kill criteria failed under emotional load
Output cites Duke / Quit by name at least once
Output ends with the user writing the criterion right now, not later
Output takes seriously the user's meta-observation ('I know that's not real') rather than dismissing it

evals.name: voice-check-user-invokes-gut
evals.prompt: I have to make a call by end of week on whether to hire this senior candidate. I've been going back and forth. My gut says yes but I can't articulate why. Should I just trust my gut?
evals.expected_output: Output should push back on 'trust your gut' unqualified — but in Duke's specific register (not rejecting intuition, insisting it must be disciplined). Should offer specific speed-triage tests (10-10-10, only-option, two-way door) as an alternative that channels the intuition into structured form. Should probably force a percentage calibration on the current gut read. Voice should be warm and teacherly (not Martin-blunt). Should end with a concrete testable action the user can do before end of week.
assertions: Output does NOT accept 'trust your gut' uncritically
Output does NOT reject intuition outright either — defends disciplined intuition (Duke's actual position)
Output introduces at least one of: 10-10-10, happiness test, only-option test, two-way door test
Output pushes for confidence calibration as a percentage
Output distinguishes reflex intuition (Nadal's forehand) from strategic-decision intuition (which needs discipline)
Output cites Duke or How to Decide by name
Output ends with a testable action the user can do this week
Response tone is warm and teacherly (not blunt/professorial) — matches Duke's voice not Martin's or Rumelt's

evals.name: considering-a-pivot-quit-decision
evals.prompt: I've been building an AI legal-research tool for 2.5 years. Raised $3M seed, burned through most of it. We have 40 law firms paying but retention is bad (60% at 12mo). My cofounder wants to pivot to insurance underwriting — she says the tech transfers and the market is bigger. I keep thinking about all we've built and I don't want to abandon the customers we do have. What do I do?
evals.expected_output: Output should (a) explicitly attack sunk cost — the $3M and 2.5 years are gone regardless; (b) name identity capture if language suggests it ('all we've built', 'don't want to abandon customers' — the latter is arguable but the emotional weight is identity-adjacent); (c) reframe the question as prospective: is the next dollar better spent on legal-research or insurance-underwriting? (d) apply the 'quitting on time feels like quitting too early' test — the discomfort the user feels is exactly what a well-timed quit feels like; (e) probably reference Butterfield/Slack (successful quit) or Wilkinson/Flow (failure to quit); (f) suggest kill criteria for the NEW path so the pattern doesn't repeat; (g) end with a concrete testable action, likely writing a kill criterion or having a specific conversation with the cofounder this week.
assertions: Output explicitly attacks sunk cost — names that the $3M and 2.5 years are gone regardless of the decision
Output reframes waste as prospective (what will the NEXT dollar produce) not retrospective
Output notices identity language OR emotional-commitment language and names it
Output applies 'quitting on time feels like quitting too early' or equivalent reframe
Output references at least one case: Butterfield/Slack, Wilkinson/Flow, Sears, or similar
Output does NOT simply recommend the pivot OR simply recommend continuing — takes seriously that this is a real hard call
Output suggests setting a kill criterion for the pivoted path so the pattern doesn't repeat
Output cites Duke / Quit by name at least once
Output ends with a specific testable action the user can take this week
Response tone is warm and non-judgmental about either path
